Title: Transcending the trust boundaries: how a cloud pentest works
Context: The assessment should answer five critical questions: Can an attacker read, modify, or delete other tenants’ data
Full Text:
Users trust a cloud provider to configure and maintain their IT services, including data storage. In turn, the provider guarantees that hosted services will stay up and that data will remain strictly confidential.

To demonstrate that their platforms are secure, providers choose different strategies: some run bug bounty programs, some rely on regular internal audits, and some bring in external research teams. However, cloud pentest methodology still has plenty of blind spots: there’s no single standard, and the outcome depends on the experience and skill of the team.

Most pentests in this area have historically focused on the external layer: the management console, customer interfaces, APIs, and the basic network perimeter. This layer is important, but it’s only the surface.

In this introductory article, we share our approach to penetration testing of cloud environments, which we’ve developed over several years and dozens of projects. We don’t claim to cover every possible scenario. Instead, we want to show the reasoning behind our pentests and highlight less obvious points that are easy to miss.

Key points

Cloud infrastructure is more complex than a traditional web application. To simplify, you can think of it as a hotel with three zones: the booking website (External, the outermost layer), the guest rooms (Overlay, the logical layer), and the staff area (Underlay, the infrastructure or base layer). A cloud service is well protected if the trust boundaries between these zones cannot be breached.

A cloud pentest’s value isn’t measured by the number of vulnerabilities found or by the mere fact that code ran. Remote command execution in an isolated tenant container is only the beginning of a pentest, not the end. The main goal is to assess whether an attacker can violate trust boundaries.

The assessment should answer five critical questions: Can an attacker read, modify, or delete other tenants’ data? Can they take over the provider’s IAM service account? Does compromising a runtime environment lead to the attack spreading to other resources and services? Can the provider’s internal resources be affected from low-trust segments? Is a virtual environment escape possible?

A negative result is still a result. If a pentester cannot move from the tenant plane to the provider overlay, that is a valuable finding. It shows which protection boundaries work in practice and which rely only on assumptions and need additional controls. However, it does not prove that the trust boundary is impossible to cross or that no other attack paths exist.

Key terms

Below, we explain some specific terms that are most often used in cloud infrastructures.

Show definitions

Tenant (think of a renter in an apartment building) is a logically isolated unit within a cloud platform. Examples include a user (such as an organization), a separate project or cloud account, or another unit of administrative and resource isolation.

Tenant plane is the set of IT services and data that a tenant manages directly: virtual machines, Kubernetes clusters, databases, object storage, and managed applications.

Management console is the graphical web interface and the entry point for the customer at the External layer.

Service runtime is the actual environment in which a provider’s cloud product runs: a process, container, pod, virtual machine, or microVM.

Service management plane consists of the provider’s internal components that create, update, restart, back up, and delete the service runtime.

IAM service account (service identity) is a special digital identity for programs, bots, cloud services, or servers. It lets them access the required cloud resources automatically and securely, without human involvement.

Context (in cloud security) is the set of attributes and credentials that define the current permissions and runtime environment of a subject in the system. It includes the identity in use (for example, a service account token, certificate, or key), the privilege level (roles and IAM policies), and the technical environment from which the request is initiated (container, virtual machine, or network segment).

Initial zone is the context in which the researcher lands right after the first successful transition. It consists of the specific runtime, IAM service account (service identity), namespace, network routes, and the set of available services.

Provider overlay is the provider’s internal environment, hidden from the customer, that is accessible from the initial zone: network segments, DNS zones, internal APIs, and management components.

Control plane consists of the platform components that make global management decisions and change the platform state: they allocate resources, assign permissions, configure the network, and coordinate state.

Data plane consists of the components that transfer or process user data and application traffic. Some components (or systems) sit at the intersection of different architectural layers, so they can’t automatically be assigned to the data plane or the control plane. Examples include logging, backup and billing systems. Their role changes depending on the task a component is performing at a given moment and how its work affects user traffic.

Cell is a bounded portion of the platform in which compute, disk, network, or management components are shared (often tied to a region, availability zone, service type, or group of tenants).

Pods are the smallest compute units in Kubernetes. A pod is one or more containers that are deployed on the same host and share common resources.

Cross-tenant impact is confirmed impact from the context of one tenant on the resources of another, without a trust relationship defined by the architecture.

Provider-level impact is impact on a provider’s management, infrastructure, or supply chain component that goes beyond the original tenant resource.

Tenant workload is the set of compute resources, processes, and applications that a customer runs and uses in their tenant to perform business tasks. It includes virtual machines, containers (such as pods in Kubernetes), serverless functions, managed databases, and any other active services that process tenant data.

What a pentester needs to check

During a project, a pentester needs to examine not only the management console but also the boundaries that separate the tenant plane from managed services and the provider’s internal infrastructure. A single request passes through many components, from the API gateway to the storage system. A configuration error in any of them changes the attack context: the researcher takes over an IAM service account, gains access to the cloud’s internal network, or acquires the ability to affect another tenant.

This is why a cloud pentest is not just a search for vulnerabilities in the management console, nor a sequential scan of cloud subnets. Above all, it means testing trust boundaries: verifying how transitions between zones with different trust levels are controlled. A more trusted zone must treat everything that comes from a less trusted zone as potentially hostile.

What makes a boundary real? Controls such as authentication and authorization (IAM, RBAC), isolation (virtualization, containerization, network segmentation), cryptography (mTLS), input handling, and others. We build a map of potential boundaries and check each one: is it actually enforced by controls, or does it rely on assumptions (architectural, infrastructural, implementation-related, and others)?

Cloud platform as a research target

When we assess the security of a traditional system, we usually start from basic architectural patterns. For web applications, this is a typical stack of a web server (Nginx, Apache, and so on), server-side logic, object storage, and integrations with third-party services. For hardware solutions, it is a chain from physical interfaces to firmware and protocol handlers.

Cloud platforms are different: how they’re actually built is highly uncertain. Cloud computing standards and reference architectures (such as NIST SP 800-145 and ISO/IEC 17788) define the roles of participants and the relationships between cloud components, but they don’t prescribe strict rules for how to build a platform.

Because there is no single technical standard, a managed database that looks the same from the outside can run in an isolated virtual machine at one provider, in a namespace of a shared Kubernetes cluster at another, and in a dedicated tenant cluster at a third. The same variability applies to software choices. A provider can use OpenStack, Kubernetes, its own control plane, or a combination of them. This means a familiar product name doesn’t give a full picture of the system’s internal structure.

That’s why a cloud pentest is harder than assessing a traditional system. Once the tenant trust boundary is breached (say, by escaping from a microVM to the host operating system), the job is no longer finding the next open port. It becomes reconstructing the architecture from indirect clues. The pentester puts the puzzle together by studying running processes, network routes, certificates, service names, and agent configurations. From these details, the researcher determines the role of each component and the trust boundaries between them.

To keep our approach vendor-agnostic, we will look at cloud infrastructure without reference to specific brands. Depending on the architectural scenario, the same component can be implemented in fundamentally different ways. For example, in one case a managed database can run as a separate managed service isolated at the virtual machine level (where the main risks are hypervisor security and the management API). In another case, it can run as a container inside a shared Kubernetes cluster (where the threat comes from the possibility of container-to-host escape and the quality of namespace isolation).

The hotel analogy and the three cloud layers

There is no single standard for building cloud infrastructure. To make pentesting systematic, we use our own three-layer model of the cloud: External, Overlay, and Underlay. The easiest way to picture a cloud platform is as a large hotel. It has a public area for guests, back-of-house areas for staff, and technical floors with utility systems. This analogy doesn’t cover every detail, but it shows well how areas of responsibility are divided and how the transitions between them work.

External layer: in a hotel, this is the booking website, the doors, and the front desk. At this layer, the pentester interacts with cloud components the way a typical user does: logs in to an account, calls the public API, creates IT services, and connects to their endpoints. Work at this layer is similar to external penetration testing or application security assessment. The main goal is to gain initial access from the outside to another customer’s tenant, or to move to the Overlay layer.

The External layer is where tenant access is provided as intended. In a hotel, the tenant is the room itself: guests control the belongings and equipment in their own room, but their key card must not open neighboring rooms. In the cloud, customers manage only their own data, virtual machines, pods, databases, object storage (S3 buckets), and accounts within their own project. A tenant is not a separate infrastructure layer. It is what the user gets at the External layer. This is where the user’s legitimate privileges end and the first trust boundary, the one the pentester checks, begins.

The provider’s service layer (Overlay): in a hotel, this is the “Staff only” area: kitchens, laundries, the control room, service corridors, and the master key system. In cloud infrastructure, this is the internal logical service management layer: runtime environments for managed services, schedulers, backup, monitoring (observability) and billing systems, the IAM system, and internal APIs. Customers use the results provided by these systems but must not get any access to them unwarranted by the architecture.

Don’t confuse this term with an overlay network in traditional network engineering: a logical network on top of a transport underlay network, such as VXLAN segments. In our methodology, Overlay has a broader meaning: it’s the internal logical layer for running and managing cloud services, and it can be split differently depending on the cloud. For clarity, the table below divides it into two sublayers: runtime environments of tenant services and provider’s internal components.

Infrastructure layer (Underlay): in a hotel, this is the utilities, electrical equipment, and physical access control systems that keep the building running. In the cloud, this is the hardware layer: physical servers, host operating systems, hypervisors, the transport network, storage systems, and out-of-band management. Careless testing at this layer can do serious damage.

But the key point of this analogy is not the rooms themselves, but the doors between them. A vulnerability on a booking website is dangerous, but a master key left in a room that opens several or every door in the building is far more so. The same rule applies in the cloud: remote code execution (RCE) inside an isolated tenant container (pod) is only a local problem. Compromise of an IAM service account that manages the resources of a region affects the entire platform.

The table below gives examples of components, pentester entry points, and assessment goals for each layer. We split the Overlay into two sublayers because the runtime environment of a tenant service and the provider’s internal infrastructure have different trust boundaries and different entry points.

A real cloud platform doesn’t always fit this matrix. A service can run in a separate virtual machine, in a pod in a shared cluster, or in a microVM. A hypervisor belongs to the Underlay, but its management API may be reachable from the Overlay. That’s why the layer a pentester is currently on (External, Overlay, or Underlay) depends not just on the IP address but on four attributes taken together:

Who controls the cloud infrastructure component.

Whose data and resources the component serves.

Which IAM service account is used for interaction.

How far its privileges extend.

Where the trust boundaries lie

When analyzing the network that supports a cloud’s internal infrastructure, it’s easy to wrongly assume there is only one trust boundary, between the tenant and the provider. But reaching the provider’s internal network may be only the first step. A real platform contains many zones with different trust levels, and compromising one component doesn’t necessarily give access to the whole infrastructure. For example, a user request may pass in sequence through the customer interface (the management console), then the tenant plane (a database), then the service runtime (the virtual machine that the database runs on), then the service management plane (an internal service that monitors database health), then the cloud control plane (an internal service that manages database resources). Only after that does it finally reach the infrastructure layer.

Each transition changes the trust zone, but it doesn’t necessarily mean reaching a new subnet or obtaining root privileges. It’s like passing through turnstiles inside the same building. We haven’t left the building (a new subnet) or gotten keys to every door (root privileges), but at each checkpoint we have our badge checked again, because different security rules apply on the other side. Sometimes the boundary lies between two roles in the same process, sometimes between an API and a worker, and sometimes between a guest virtual machine and a hypervisor. At the boundary between an API and a worker, a vulnerability can arise from differences in data handling. For example, an internal cloud API accepts a string containing a null byte (\x00) from a user, considers it valid, and passes it on. A background worker then blindly trusts this data and inserts it into a low-level query to a PostgreSQL database. In C libraries, \x00 terminates a string. As a result, the database handler truncates the text at the point where this byte was injected. This breaks the logic of the SQL query or permission check and resets the regular user’s context. The system is then forced to change the password of the main administrator (postgres), which leads to full database takeover.

Example 1. Strict isolation (managed database)

A customer rents a managed database in their tenant. The tenant is allowed to run SQL queries but not allowed to connect to the operating system the database runs on. Here, the trust boundary lies between the permissions of a database role and the runtime environment of the database process. If, through the permitted SQL queries, the pentester manages to reach code execution at the operating system level as the service process, the pentester gains full access to the host’s resources. This lets them do more than just collect information. They can actively interact with the host: read and modify files, analyze running processes, establish network connections to internal services, and extract credentials (for example, an IAM service account token) to attack other cloud components.

Example 2. Legitimate access (managed virtual machine)

In another implementation, the provider supports SSH key authentication by design, and the user connects to the resource like to any other virtual machine. Formally, the product is still called a “managed database”, but the actual trust boundary shifts deeper, to the level where the guest OS interacts with the host infrastructure. In this case, SSH access to the operating system is not a violation in itself, because the service model allows it. What we need to test is the next boundary, the one between the service virtual machine and the management agents, metadata, host, or control plane.

This leads to several practical rules:

Normal execution of user code does not, by itself, prove an isolation breach. In IT services such as interactive notebooks, continuous integration (CI) runners, or serverless systems, code execution is a product feature.

Gaining maximum privileges inside a pod does not mean gaining maximum privileges on the node. After crossing each trust boundary (for example, into a zone with different privileges or service accounts), you need to re-check what’s visible: processes, mount points, interfaces, devices, and IAM service accounts.

An IAM service account token that a researcher finds is not necessarily useful. What matters is who issued it and which systems accept it. The tenant or service the token is bound to, and the actions it permits there, also matter.

The fact that a tenant container can reach a provider’s internal IP address does not mean a compromise has occurred. In many clouds, some internal services are reachable over the network by design. For a real compromise, an attacker must either steal a service token or find an internal service that mistakenly accepts customer accounts or requires no authentication.

Remote code execution inside the environment where a service runs does not mean access to the control plane. This is only the initial zone, from which the researcher must look for the next trust boundary: service tokens, the provider’s internal APIs, and neighboring containers.

To tell a real trust boundary violation from a false positive, we use four sequential stages from the researcher’s perspective:

Network visibility. The researcher can see the provider’s internal service from the tenant plane. This is not a breach yet, but it is the first sign that isolation may be insufficient.

The researcher manages to authenticate to a service by presenting a token or certificate compromised at the previous step (for example, a service account token or a metadata token). This is serious, because the service treats the request as legitimate.

The target object grants specific permissions to the current context. This is not yet the execution of dangerous operations, but only a check that they are allowed.

Controlled action beyond the original trust boundary. The researcher performs the minimum safe action that confirms the previously obtained permissions work in practice. For example, they create a test record in a neighboring tenant (usually a second test tenant).

The first two stages only produce a hypothesis that the trust boundary has been violated. The object is visible on the network and accepts requests, but that does not mean the researcher can change anything in it. Confirmed impact appears only in the last two stages, when the researcher obtains authorization and performs a controlled action beyond the original boundary. For example, network reachability of a neighboring database indicates insufficient network isolation, but cross-tenant impact appears only when the researcher can use the original context to perform an action on another tenant’s resource that the cloud model doesn’t allow, such as reading data. To keep the test ethical, the researcher demonstrates such reading only between their own test accounts, so real users’ data stays confidential.

Attacker model and three research goals

Dividing the cloud infrastructure into three layers (External, Overlay, and Underlay) helps define the attacker model for each layer. In penetration testing, the researcher can focus on one layer and look for every possible way to violate the nearest trust boundary. Another approach is to build a full attack chain across all layers. The attacker model also defines the starting point: the access level and position from which the pentest begins. Below is a general list of attacker models that apply to most cloud infrastructures:

External attacker without an account. The test covers the public attack surface, registration, the login mechanism, externally accessible services, and the path to the first tenant context. Layer: External.

Attacker with legitimate tenant access. This is the key model for a multi-tenant cloud: the tenant is entitled to create their own resources and tries to go beyond the limits those resources impose. Layer: External.

Internal attacker with a compromised runtime. The starting point is a compromised process, pod, or virtual machine. This scenario is especially relevant for supply chain attacks. The researcher explores options for lateral movement in the network and host environment. Layer: Overlay or Underlay.

Internal attacker with a compromised IAM service account token or an operator account. This model involves testing IAM and the cloud platform management processes. Layer: Overlay or Underlay.

Regardless of the attacker model and the initial entry point, the research goals at the initial stage fall into three groups.

1. Code execution first

The goal of this approach is to execute arbitrary code inside a provider-managed environment. To do this, a pentester can attack a managed database, serverless function, CI/CD workload, PaaS application, tenant virtual machine, container, or virtual network gateway.

Example of an attack chain through a managed service The pentester interacts with the managed service interface and finds a vulnerability in it (for example, CVE-2026-19478 in the case of the GitLab web interface) or in add-on modules deployed by the cloud provider. The vulnerability allows the researcher to execute code remotely inside the runtime (operating system), find an IAM service account, and use it to gain access to the resource management service. The researcher can then look for vulnerabilities in that service and penetrate the provider overlay.

Example of an attack chain through a virtual environment The chain begins with the compromise of a tenant workload. The researcher plants malicious code in a popular OS or container image in advance. A cloud tenant downloads and runs the trojanized image, and the attacker gains access inside that specific container. Next, the attacker finds ways to escape the container (using CVE-2026-43284) into the runtime: the container runtime, hypervisor, or host agent. From there, they reach the host shared with other containers and can affect the provider’s management components.

2. Credentials first

Rather than gaining access to a runtime environment, the researcher may obtain credentials that cloud services accept as valid: a service account token, metadata access credentials, an mTLS certificate, a bootstrap token, or an object storage key.

In this scenario, the move into the provider overlay doesn’t come from breaking network isolation. It happens through legitimate platform functionality. The network may be well segmented, but an over-privileged IAM service account token that the attacker manages to extract (for example, from environment variables or metadata) can legitimately call an internal API through a standard gateway or token exchange service.

3. Administrative or service context

The goal of this scenario is to bypass technical restrictions by gaining legitimate access through channels intended for staff. The route often starts with targeting people (phishing, insiders, or leaked employee or contractor credentials). However, the final entry point into the internal environment is technical: a connection through the operator’s VPN, a support portal, a remote support tool, an administrative workstation, an SSH certificate, or a serial console. Although the route often starts with compromising a person, the resulting initial zone (the technical context with certain privileges and access to resources where the researcher ends up) can match the first scenario. For example, access to a managed database host (DBaaS host) can be obtained not by exploiting a vulnerability but through a legitimate administrative channel, which is then used for privilege escalation.

Sorting out the architectural zoo

After moving deeper into the cloud infrastructure and gaining access to a node, the pentester analyzes local artifacts. Completely different architectures can hide behind the same managed service.

OpenStack-like infrastructure

IaaS services based on OpenStack usually include a large set of components: an IAM service account, compute resources, networking, images and block storage, as well as API processes, workers, a message broker, and platform state databases. A managed service built on top of such an IaaS layer can use a separate virtual machine for each database instance, several instances on a shared virtual machine, a Kubernetes cluster on virtual workers, or even a dedicated tenant for a specific product.

A message broker such as RabbitMQ is typical for OpenStack, but finding one doesn’t prove that the target is a stock OpenStack deployment. The provider may have changed the trust model, added its own API, and replaced some of the components.

Kubernetes-based platforms

In clouds of this type, a central Kubernetes cluster controls the entire infrastructure: not only containers but also virtual machines, other tenant Kubernetes clusters, and managed services. At the service runtime level, a product can run as a pod in a shared namespace, an application inside a tenant, a KubeVirt virtual machine, or a worker node of a separate cluster. From the outside, they all look like the same product, but their trust boundaries and the attack surface behind them differ radically.

Because the platform is managed through a Kubernetes cluster, where the service account token is the main unit of authorization, it’s especially important to determine where the IAM service account you obtained during the pentest lives: in a tenant cluster, in a managed cluster, or with an operator that serves multiple tenants. Identical-looking tokens may have permissions for only one pod, or they may allow changing resources in several environments at once.

Custom control plane and configuration management systems

A provider may forgo off-the-shelf platforms altogether. For example, in this kind of architecture, a provider might build its public API in-house, deploy virtual machines through libvirt or a lightweight IaaS layer, automate networking with scripts around Open vSwitch (OVS), build object storage on Ceph, and distribute node configuration through SaltStack or another configuration management system.

In this architecture, a virtual machine management service might get its settings from an internal HTTP service, a script with shared credentials might run backups, billing might receive events from a queue, and an internal agent might talk to the control plane over mTLS. Almost every component here is specific to the provider. The main risk area is not vulnerabilities in well-known products, such as those built on open-source solutions, but logic errors at the junctions between internal systems.

Mixed-stack platform

In practice, the most common setup is a mix of approaches

The infrastructure core (IaaS layer) is built on OpenStack

Kubernetes runs the managed services

The storage system runs on Ceph

IAM, billing systems, and the internal API are custom-built.

Here are some clues that can help form initial hypotheses about the environment:

A Kubernetes token and cluster DNS in the runtime environment of the host under investigation suggest that the service is running in the context of a pod.

A running qemu-guest-agent process indicates that we are inside a virtual machine rather than on a physical server.

Attached Ceph/RBD volumes point to a separate storage plane in the platform architecture, implemented as distributed block storage.

A large number of CNI or Open vSwitch (OVS) network interfaces means that this is a shared Kubernetes node

However, any such clue needs additional verification tests.

Example of a mixed-stack cloud platform

How to choose the next trust boundary

After the pentester has examined the initial zone, the next route depends on a combination of two factors:

Network visibility: which segments, services, and tenants are reachable.

Available trust level: which credentials, certificates, and API methods are accepted as valid in those segments.

Sometimes the network has almost no restrictions, but all services require correct mTLS authentication. Title: Citrus Ransomware: VLESS for traffic, Sn00py for encryption, and LLMs lending a hand
Context: The PowerShell scripts run through this file included an exploit for the CVE-2020-1337 vulnerability; the same exploit is available in the Metasploit GitHub repository
Full Text:
In recent years, cyberthreats have increasingly taken a hybrid approach, combining time-tested techniques for advancing through infrastructure, modern methods of evading network filters, and automation powered by large language models. This is also the approach of Citrus Ransomware, a previously undocumented group whose toolset includes VLESS tunnels (used to disguise traffic as regular HTTPS) and a ransomware Trojan from the Sn00py family. The attackers also integrate LLMs (large language models) into the process of infrastructure compromise.

In this article, we review the tactics and techniques the group used in recent incidents.

Initial Access: attacks through contractors

The attackers gain initial access to victims’ infrastructure through compromised contractors. They use credentials stolen from these contractors’ employees to connect to corporate VPNs or directly to internet-facing terminal servers over RDP.

Execution: commands, LLMs, and Impacket

The attackers run commands on compromised systems through the standard Windows command interpreter and PowerShell. As the attack progresses, they create and run PowerShell scripts, batch files, and commands generated by LLMs. One example of the latter is the commands below, which disable the account of one of the administrators.

Comment translation

# Disable account # Verify result

Both commands come with comments, something attackers rarely bother with, so the comments very likely point to LLM use. And the models did more than generate commands. The attackers also produced full scripts, complete with the comments typical of LLM output.

Comment translation

# Creating background tasks for each computer with a thread limit # Concurrent task limit control # Quick ping

The fragment above comes from a script Citrus used to enumerate active user sessions on domain systems.

Besides LLMs, the attackers use atexec, a classic tool from the Impacket collection, to create scheduled tasks that run commands on hosts:

We did not see the exact commands behind these tasks, but Group Policy was refreshed after they ran, so they most likely executed gpupdate /force.

When the group compromises 1C:Enterprise servers, it uses external data processors (1C-Shell) to run commands.

Persistence: scheduled tasks

Citrus uses scheduled tasks to launch its malicious tools automatically. The attackers create the tasks manually through PowerShell:

On systems that are not regularly rebooted, such as terminal servers, they sometimes run their tools without establishing persistence at all.

Privilege Escalation: vulnerabilities and configuration flaws

In every case we know of, the contractor domain account used for initial access had very limited privileges, so the attackers tried to escalate them.

To do this, they attempted to exploit the authentication bypass vulnerability CVE-2026-54121 (Certighost); these attempts created machine accounts with telltale names in Active Directory, such as:

GHOSTAUFTAFGS

GHOSTCZYQVAZS

GHOSTIVPRLDZA

GHOST{8 random letters}

These names are generated by scripts making use of an exploit published on GitHub.

The exploit works like this: on behalf of the newly created account, it requests a certificate based on the Machine template from the system holding the AD CS role. The Attributes, Subject, and SubjectAlternativeName fields contain parameters like these:

<Data Name='Attributes'>CertificateTemplate:Machine\nSAN:dns=dc01.victim.domain\ncdc:91.210.109[.]118\nrmd:dc01.victim.domain </Data> <Data Name='Subject'>CN=GHOSTABUIEFAD.victim.domain</Data> <Data Name='SubjectAlternativeName'>DNS name =dc01.victim.domain\r\n</Data>

The cdc attribute specifies the IP address or name of the system that the certification authority must contact to verify the data. The attackers specify the address of a system they control (in this case, 91.210.109[.]118) and send forged data from it. If exploitation succeeds, the certification authority issues a certificate with the specified parameters, based on the specified template.

Once the certificate is issued, the domain controller name in its SubjectAlternativeName field lets the attackers authenticate as the domain controller account.

In one case, the attackers also uploaded an executable for persistence, on behalf of which PowerShell scripts were launched with nonstandard HostName (Имя узла) field value.

Although the file was later deleted, indirect evidence hints at its purpose. For example, the MSFConsole value may indicate that the file is a component of the Metasploit framework. The PowerShell scripts run through this file included an exploit for the CVE-2020-1337 vulnerability; the same exploit is available in the Metasploit GitHub repository.

Beyond classic vulnerabilities in Microsoft products, the attackers also took an interest in 1C:Enterprise servers with insecure configurations (article in Russian).

On top of the configuration flaws, 1C:Enterprise systems are frequently accessed by support staff and administrators who hold elevated privileges in Active Directory. Together, these factors make it easy for attackers to escalate privileges and start moving laterally.

Stealth: covering tracks and masquerading

To hinder incident response, the attackers delete their tools and output files and clear the command history.

While the tools are still in use in the victim’s infrastructure, the attackers typically give them and their auxiliary objects legitimate-looking names:

KasperskyGPO_Deploy_64.exe and KasperskyGPO_Deploy_64_FIXED.exe are self-extracting archives. They contain the Deploy-KasperskyGPO.ps1 script, a directory with a malicious Group Policy Object, and one of two archives, KasperskyAgent.exe or agent.exe.

KasperskyAgentInstaller.exe, KasperskyAgent.exe, and agent.exe are self-extracting archives containing the ransomware Trojan executable and auxiliary files.

Kaspersky GPO is the name of the Group Policy Object that distributes the ransomware Trojan in the victim’s infrastructure.

KasperskyAgentInstallTask and Sysvc are names used for the scheduled task that runs the self-extracting ransomware archive files.

Deploy-KasperskyGPO.ps1 is the PowerShell script that creates the malicious Kaspersky GPO.

Kaspersky_GPO_Deployment.log is the log of the Deploy-KasperskyGPO.ps1 script.

Note that using the Kaspersky name in malicious file names doesn’t help the attackers avoid detection. Kaspersky solutions successfully detect and block these malicious files.

Defense Impairment: weak access policies for security tools play into attackers’ hands

To stay under the radar longer, the attackers clear event logs on some systems using the built-in wevtutil utility.

In addition, once they have sufficient privileges, they disable antivirus protection on hosts, which lets them run tools such as mimikatz.

The attackers also go after the centralized management consoles for security solutions, which they then use to disable protection en masse.

At the Impact stage, the attackers also use a Group Policy Object that modifies Windows Defender settings in the registry to switch it off. As a result, the antivirus did not respond when the ransomware was launched.

Finally, if they have sufficient privileges, the attackers manually add their malicious tools to the antivirus exclusion list.

Credential Access: mimikatz, a keylogger, and extraction of credentials from files

To capture keystrokes on a compromised system, the attackers use a modified version of the peeping-tom keylogger, whose source code is available on GitHub. The keylogger executable and its log file are located at the following paths:

C:\ProgramData\Oracle\Java\jhost.exe

C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\CLR\ErrorLog.txt

In the sample we found, stolen data was sent to 91.210.109[.]118. Persistence for the keylogger is provided by the scheduled task described above in the Persistence section.

To dump credentials from memory, the attackers use mimikatz. Files related to mimikatz are located at the following paths:

C:\ProgramData\x64\mimidrv.sys

C:\ProgramData\x64\mimikatz.exe

C:\ProgramData\x64\mimilib.dll

C:\ProgramData\x64\mimispool.dll

To hunt for credentials and other secrets (SSH keys, access tokens, and the like) in files on accessible network shares, the group uses Snaffler. To simplify running the tool, the attackers drop a configuration file on the system:

Besides data from network shares, the attackers were interested in data stored in password managers (for example, KeePass) on administrator workstations.

Discovery: the standard toolkit

Local discovery

After gaining control of a compromised system, the attackers ran a basic set of commands to identify the current user, running processes, network interface settings, the system’s external IP address, and so on:

whoami tasklist quser ipconfig curl 2ip[.]io

Remote discovery

In the early stages, the attackers used the fscan scanner to gather information on the internal infrastructure. They were particularly interested in the following ports:

135 (RPC)

139 (NetBIOS-SSN)

1433 (Microsoft SQL)

8006 (Proxmox VE)

Once they had the access they needed and had moved laterally, the attackers ran ADRecon on domain controllers and SharpHound on one of the workstations.

The attackers also used PowerShell to run LDAP queries against the controllers of adjacent domains, pulling lists of domain systems, users, and groups.

Russian text translation

The user has no additional groups in memberOf (primary only) User not found

As an alternative to PowerShell, the attackers used the net.exe utility to get information about domain users and privileged groups:

net users /domain net group "Domain Admins" /domain net group "Администраторы домена" /domain

Lateral Movement: SSH, RDP, and WinRM

For lateral movement, the group relies on standard remote administration protocols: SSH, WinRM, and RDP. The attackers connect to systems either through previously deployed tunnels or directly from the compromised host.

Command and Control: delivering tools to the system

To deliver its tools to target hosts, the group uses built-in OS utilities. Specifically, the incidents involved:

certutil:

The Windows BITS background service (invoked in two ways):

cURL:

PowerShell:

Creating tunnels with Xray

The certutil and BITS commands shown above are what the attackers used to download Xray onto victim systems. They then used Xray to set up reverse VLESS tunnels to the command-and-control server. The configuration file, stored alongside the Xray executable, was usually named config.json. In some cases, the attackers deleted it right after starting the tunnel to hide the Xray configuration from defenders.

Judging by the configuration files recovered during the analysis, the attackers used port 443 on the VLESS server to blend in with legitimate HTTPS traffic. The configuration files also contain blocks that set up the REALITY protocol, which is intended to disguise the attackers’ traffic as requests to the legitimate site mirror.yandex.ru:

The traffic was also disguised as requests to another legitimate site, yastatic.net:

Installing AnyDesk

The PowerShell command above AnyDesk, which the attackers used to remotely control compromised hosts.

After the download, the attackers installed the software with the --silent flag to avoid alerting the user, set a connection password, and used PowerShell to pull the infected machine’s ID (which AnyDesk uses for remote connections on the client side) from the configuration file:

Collection & Exfiltration: data from messaging apps

Right before encrypting the data, the attackers connected to one of the domain controllers and ran the PowerShell script steal_tgs.ps1, which created the tdatas directory. According to the NTFS USN journal, while the script ran, 7-Zip created archives in this directory with telltale names hinting at their contents:

<system_name>_<date>_<username>_tdata.zip

The directory name tdatas and the substring tdata may refer to the C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Roaming\Telegram Desktop\tdata directory. The Telegram messaging app uses this directory to store authorization keys, session data, app settings, and other session information.

So the attackers were harvesting messaging app data from remote systems they could reach, packing it with 7-Zip and uploading it to an external web service through Google Chrome.

Impact: Sn00py ransomware Trojan

The Citrus group uses ransomware from the Sn00py family to encrypt data. It’s written in Go and uses the RSA-2048 and ChaCha20 algorithms to encrypt user files (but not system files) on Windows systems. Encrypted files receive the .citrus extension. For now, decryption is impossible without the attackers’ private key.

When launched, the ransomware opens a console on the victim’s device, where it outputs the commands it runs. It also attempts to modify the boot configuration data (BCD) by invoking a nonexistent executable, bcedit (likely a typo for bcdedit):

The ransomware’s console output contains the string:

We`re going to do something special today :). Made with RaaS platform Sn00py.

The string likely means the ransomware is distributed under the ransomware-as-a-service model, where attackers don’t write the malware themselves but subscribe to a ready-made offering.

The ransomware configuration contains the Citrus group’s public key in the pubkey parameter:

-----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY----- A7+eV3M+EDIh5kId+vf46QkKpAOKxUxv97PDFj66ox+uE0GV9UQhrSmBAoGAcyNI +z7noIwrFYnHi6wtj8gLEOT0hE/cNDp0VLoUnAzi551kZA7J3Q575jwqrJcDrZSO JLkZX7pxLLSd9iQdxMxDrLYZGRtiht8ToD5OGZri36oPvnW56ijJZ/NMzlFtVr7V iSZJr5Qkz2cxShcSuhDLLXmzleclBd7HQtWTuZUCgYEAqN8WFAZxkV2e1p4v3U98 VOu4XxEfqAc2Gs2Ccs/kkWoX/1fxvuSRcF6/hMdfVwUP0z+/fnhbFMNfysBeWo1W ZfmpBF/HbnRSg2ZDLWIwXEXEsNNSRmlvwyHWSEZgyG1xjgjSZKWuxo92WVmPxb5i S6NLrZkHPHwqaBy8CnD6ft8= -----END PUBLIC KEY-----

The host_blacklist parameter also lists the system names that are exempt from encryption:

[ "DC01", "DC02", "DC03", "DC04" ]

This list includes the domain controllers used to distribute the policy that launches the ransomware. This way, the attackers ensure the policy keeps propagating uninterrupted.

As it runs, the Trojan drops CITRUS_README.txt files containing the ransom note:

-[ All your data were encrypted ] | |-If you try to decrypt them yourself, you will lose your data. To decrypt all systems, you need to contact us for guidance and a data recovery tool in the future. If you ignore our offer and the conversation does not take place, we will take extreme measures against your company and your employees, as a result of which you will lose access to all resources of your network and lose your reputation. | |-To contact us - register your mail here: https://account.proton.me/mail/signup?plan=free and write to us by email: [REDACTED] |-Further negotiations regarding this situation will be conducted there. Also we have Telegram: [REDACTED] | |-Be sure to use a VPN, and do not attempt to write from other email addresses, as there is a high chance that the messages will not be delivered to either party. | |-You have 72 hours to contact us to establish negotiations and interaction, starting from the date of creation of this file. |-If you do not contact us within 3 days, we will consider this a refusal to cooperate. This will entail immediate measures, such as: Dumps of your services, personal data of employees, accounting, contracts and source code. | |-Warning: \\_ Do not delete, modify, or attempt to recover files by any means other than using our key and decryptor. This will damage your data, and we cannot guarantee its recovery. \\_ Do not try to make this public, as you will only harm yourself and your reputation.

As mentioned above, the group uses malicious Group Policy Objects to launch the ransomware across victim systems en masse. The GPOs are created by self-extracting archives, of which we have seen two versions. Each archive contains:

A self-extracting archive with the ransomware Trojan and auxiliary files.

A directory containing the Group Policy Object. The policy drops the ransomware archive on the target system, creates a scheduled task that runs the archive with the parameters /quiet /norestart, enables the WinRM service, and disables the Volume Shadow Copy service and Windows Defender antivirus protection. It also sets a desktop wallpaper displaying the ransom note.

A PowerShell script that copies the ransomware archive to the \\<current_domain_name>\SYSVOL directory on the domain controller and links the malicious GPO to the domain using the Import-GPO and New-GPLink

One version of the PowerShell script contained comments suggesting that it was likely edited with an LLM:

Links to Toy Ghouls

While analyzing Citrus activity, we noticed several similarities to Toy Ghouls. Although their infrastructures don’t directly overlap, the two groups share TTPs: they encrypt their victims’ systems, use a similar set of tools (1C-Shell for remote command execution on 1C:Enterprise servers, mimikatz, PsExec, and ADRecon), and store these tools in the same directories. What’s more, both groups are Russian-speaking and attack Russian companies only. In several incidents, we saw the same infrastructure compromised simultaneously by both Toy Ghouls and Citrus.

Conclusion

What makes Citrus interesting is its unconventional approach to network tunneling and its use of AI to generate auxiliary tools. Even so, the attackers largely rely on well-known tools and techniques, which makes early detection somewhat easier. Kaspersky solutions detect all the activity described in this article.

That said, the Citrus attacks are another reminder that contractor access to an organization’s infrastructure must be tightly controlled and restricted. After all, compromising contractor accounts is exactly how the attackers get into their victims’ networks. We’ll continue to track the group’s activity and report new techniques as we discover them.

Title: Key benefits of Zero Trust Network Access over corporate VPN access | Kaspersky official blog
Context: For example, in the October attacks on Ivanti Connect Secure gateways, the APT group UTA0576 chained three zero-day vulnerabilities to compromise a fully patched device
Full Text:
The tried-and-true recipe for protecting a corporate network has become far less effective than it once was. Guarding the perimeter with a firewall and granting remote access through a VPN gateway has become both cumbersome and risky: day to day, it’s hard to configure how users and cloud services interact, and during cyberattacks the VPN gateway is now a prime target. According to data from insurer At-Bay, nearly three-quarters of the successful ransomware attacks in its 2025 analysis began with a compromised VPN.

To jointly improve network security and operational efficiency, companies need to rethink the remote access model itself. The end goal is a secure connection between an employee and work resources. That by no means implies that an employee (or someone posing as one) should get full access to the corporate network.

What recent VPN attacks show

VPN technology itself isn’t fatally outdated — as long as you treat it as a way to encrypt and tunnel traffic. The problem is how VPN is most commonly deployed: a user authenticates at the entry point, lands on the company network, and from there restrictions (if there are any) depend on segmentation, firewalls, and the protection of individual systems. Inside the network, behind the VPN gateway, a user can reach a wide range of internal services with minimal restrictions. Often, the VPN gateway itself is a privileged device, and successfully compromising it gives attackers many ways to take over the network.

For example, in the October attacks on Ivanti Connect Secure gateways, the APT group UTA0576 chained three zero-day vulnerabilities to compromise a fully patched device. After gaining root privileges, they used the VPN’s own legitimate service account to query the domain controller and collect passwords and BitLocker recovery keys.

Before that, vulnerabilities in Check Point and SonicWall gateways were similarly exploited, with the SonicWall attacks carried out by the Akira ransomware operators.

Remote work, VPNs, and stolen data

Today, depending on the country, between 12% and 30% of employees work from home either full or part-time. This shift has significantly increased the number of IT systems that need to be reachable from outside the organizations’ networks — often from personal devices. Personal devices are far more likely than corporate ones to get infected with infostealers. As a result, the black market is flooded with corporate credentials stolen from such computers: it represents 30% of everything initial access brokers (IABs) sell.

Even over a VPN, a strictly segmented network can grant only very limited access. But in practice, exceptions pile up over years of operation: a contractor needs access to a whole subnet, an admin gets “everything, temporarily”, an old application needs a few more ports. These exceptions piled up especially fast during the covid pandemic. As a result, a stolen account often opens the door not to a single service but to the entire infrastructure.

VPN administration overhead

For VPN access to work properly and securely, configuring the VPN gateway alone is usually not enough: you have to set up MFA, device posture checks, network segmentation, and log collection separately. Then you have to make all of it work together. A new employee or application may require changes in several systems at once. Each system works correctly on its own, but the rules drift apart, and figuring out why a certain user has no access turns into a tour of five consoles.

What switching to Zero Trust Network Access changes

First and foremost, Zero Trust Network Access (ZTNA) changes the access model itself and its basic unit of access. Instead of “this user has access rights to this subnet”, a ZTNA system makes decisions like “this user, on this device, in this location, who has passed these levels of verification, can access this specific application”.

Such a decision takes into account a combination of factors (identity, device, and so on) that the policy specifies. The right to work with a ticketing system or a customer database shouldn’t automatically let someone connect to a file server or a domain controller.

Depending on the policies, a ZTNA system can grant access to the needed resource behind the scenes through a combination of methods: a dedicated VPN tunnel to a specific internal server, a reverse connection from a corporate application in a private cloud, and others. A legitimate user doesn’t need to know any of this, but an attacker’s ability to move around the network and attack new services will be severely limited.

Keep in mind that ZTNA is a specific tool — just one part of a broader zero trust architecture. Buying a single product doesn’t mean a company has implemented zero trust.

Benefits of switching from a traditional VPN to ZTNA

A well-implemented ZTNA system primarily reduces the potential damage (the blast radius) if part of the infrastructure or someone’s credentials get compromised; at the same time, deploying it also noticeably decreases an attacker’s room to maneuver.

Reducing the risk of gateway attacks

A VPN gateway usually accepts any connection from the internet. Before verifying the user, the gateway closely analyzes incoming connections, cryptographic messages, and requests to its management and authentication portals. A gateway vulnerability lets an attacker run detailed reconnaissance against the system at this stage and bypass authentication altogether.

Some ZTNA architectures reduce this exposure. An internal connector establishes an outbound connection to a cloud broker on its own. The user connects to the broker separately, and access to the application opens after the necessary checks. In such a system, there’s no need to expose your own gateway for remote access at all.

In a ZTNA architecture with a self-hosted broker, you can’t shift the risk to the ZTNA provider. But a number of ZTNA solutions significantly reduce the attack surface of a self-hosted broker too, for example by using Single Packet Authorization. The broker doesn’t process any requests until it receives a correctly formed encrypted packet, which the client uses to prove its authenticity up front.

Limiting the consequences of compromised credentials and workstations

ZTNA can tie access not only to a password but also to the state of the device: whether the organization manages it, whether its certificate is valid, whether the OS is up to date, whether the security software’s databases are up to date, and whether there are any signs of compromise. What’s more, ZTNA can authenticate the same user differently for different tasks. Does the user just want to read the news on the internal portal, and is the computer they log in from already known about? A password is enough. Is the user logging in to a software repository to change application source code, or opening the budget planning system? Then they’ll have to pass phishing-resistant authentication, for example with a hardware key (such as a YubiKey). If the connection type or other parameters change, the user will even have to re-authenticate.

It’s easy to see how a hypothetical infostealer attack gets more complicated in this scenario. It’s not enough to simply steal a password or a browser session. Trying to use them on a new device will cut the connection.

Here, ZTNA functions partly overlap with what EDR and MDM/EMM agents do on the device. That’s why several vendors bundle these capabilities into a single agent. At the same time, ZTNA limits the consequences of an attack but doesn’t replace endpoint protection. If an attacker uses a remote access Trojan (RAT) rather than an infostealer and directly controls an employee’s device, the ZTNA agent may not be able to tell the attacker’s actions from the employee’s.

Improving observability and detecting anomalies faster

When an employee works from home over a VPN, the firewalls, web filters, and SIEM/XDR often see only shallow network telemetry. That’s why, for example, the actions of the Qilin ransomware operators — who exploited an authentication vulnerability in Palo Alto GlobalProtect (CVE-2026-0257) — were hard to tell apart from legitimate employee activity.

ZTNA lets you tie access events to specific identities: users, devices, and applications. Depending on the implementation, SOC teams may get connection logs and, for supported protocols, logs of individual requests to specific applications.

With this level of log detail and the right SIEM rules in place, anomalies quickly catch SOC analysts’ attention.

Simplifying access administration

“Guest” and “temporary” VPN access is a perennial headache for IT and infosec teams. Contractor accounts are created as temporary but stay active for years. In 2026, attackers breached a large European financial institution through this kind of poorly controlled access. ZTNA makes just-in-time (JIT) access possible. A contractor’s support engineer gets access only to the web interface of the one server they need, and that access shuts off automatically after a set time (say, two hours or two days).

Reducing regulatory and insurance risks

Both regulators and the cyber-insurance market are pushing for stricter access management. In April 2026, CISA explicitly named standing contractor VPN access as one of the critical threats to industrial networks. Insurers are also reacting to this trend: organizations with outdated VPN configurations are increasingly hit with rising insurance premiums.

A quick plan for migrating from VPN to ZTNA

Overall, the migration plan looks like this:

Take inventory of your remote access: VPNs, RDP servers, vendor gateways, service accounts, and configured firewall exceptions.

Design and fully document an access structure built around applications and roles instead of the familiar subnets.

Review and, if needed, improve your granular system for identifying users, devices, and applications (identity management), since effective ZTNA depends on it. Enable phishing-resistant MFA, and set up policies for access recovery, posture checks, and session revocation.

Outline an isolated pilot scenario that’s relatively easy to implement but not trivial. For example, start with contractor access to a few applications.

Gradually extend ZTNA to new groups of employees and services.

After each migration stage, disable or significantly restrict the access methods that are no longer needed. For the VPNs that remain, apply strict segmentation and monitoring.

Some legacy applications, industrial systems, and site-to-site connections will still need VPN for a long time to come. The goal isn’t to remove those three letters from your infrastructure at any cost, but to make sure VPN gateways stop being an easy target and an effective launchpad for attacks on your network.

Ransomware

Quarterly trends and highlights

Threat actor disruption

In August, the creator and lead administrator of the Ransom Cartel ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) operation was sentenced to 16 years in prison. The convict developed the ransomware Trojan and at the time of his arrest played a central role in the RaaS operation: running the affiliate program, recruiting affiliates, supplying them with information and attack tools, working with initial access brokers, communicating with victims, and processing payments.

In September, a member of the Ryuk RaaS group was sentenced to two years in prison and three years of supervised release. In 2019 and 2020, he and his accomplices breached organizations’ networks and encrypted data with the Ryuk Trojan. According to public reports, hundreds of workstations and servers were compromised. According to the prosecution, the attacker received a total of about 1610 BTC in ransom payments from victims.

Also in September, a member of the Conti RaaS group was sentenced to four years in prison. He was charged with attacking companies in 2021 and 2022. In addition to carrying out attacks, he developed part of the group’s malware toolkit.

Vulnerabilities and attacks

In July, researchers published a report on the Qilin group exploiting the CVE-2026-0257 vulnerability in Palo Alto Networks firewall software. The vulnerability allowed attackers to bypass authentication and compromise victims’ networks without valid accounts.

CISA published information in its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog (KEV) on several CVEs actively exploited by ransomware groups:

CVE-2026-15409/CVE-2026-15410 in SonicWall SMA1000 remote access gateways. CISA doesn’t specify which groups exploited these vulnerabilities, but researchers have linked this activity to INC Ransom.

CVE-2026-45659 in Microsoft SharePoint Server allowed an authenticated, low-privileged attacker to achieve remote code execution.

CVE-2025-60710 in Microsoft Windows allowed attackers to escalate privileges locally.

CVE-2026-59310 in VMware vCenter enabled unauthenticated remote code execution.

CVE-2025-14733 in WatchGuard Firebox also enabled unauthenticated remote code execution.

CVE-2026-63077 in JetBrains TeamCity allowed OS commands to run with the privileges of the TeamCity server process by way of an authentication bypass through the agent polling protocol. Command execution at that level could give access to configurations, credentials, CI/CD pipelines, and more.

IT threat evolution in Q3 2026. Non-mobile statistics IT threat evolution in Q3 2026. Mobile statistics

The mobile section of the quarterly cyberthreat report includes statistics on malware, adware, and potentially unwanted software for Android, as well as descriptions of the most notable threats for Android and iOS discovered during the reporting period. These statistics are based on detection alerts from Kaspersky products, collected from users who consented to provide statistical data to Kaspersky Security Network.

The quarter in figures

According to Kaspersky Security Network, in Q3 2026:

More than 1.66 million attacks involving mobile malware, adware, or unwanted software were blocked.

The Trojan-Banker category was the prevalent mobile malware threat with a 31.63% share of all detected malicious apps.

Over 378,000 malicious installation packages were detected, including 119,688 mobile banking Trojan packages.

Quarterly highlights

In July, we discovered a malicious app targeting Brazilian users that may have used AI to automate fraud. The app was disguised as Google Play Protect, a suite of security services for Android devices.

Malicious app imitating Google Play Protect

The app’s code used the DistilBERT model to interpret natural-language commands sent from the C2 server. Traces left in the code suggest the server-side commands may also have been generated by a large language model (LLM).

In August, we discovered a Trojan that analyzed images saved in the device’s gallery and took screenshots to look for banking data, including CVV codes. The malware used an on-device AI model to classify images. The app could also update this model, which gave the scammers a way to expand the Trojan’s functionality.

In the third quarter, the infamous subscription Trojan detected as Trojan.AndroidOS.Subscriber.bh made it into Google Play again. This time, it was disguised as an app for creating keyboard themes.

Subscription Trojan disguised as a keyboard theme app

The Trojan opened a subscription link in a hidden WebView and intercepted the message containing the confirmation code. According to our data, the scammers mainly targeted users in Thailand.

There were also new attacks on iOS users. In August, researchers at Socket discovered 13 infected PHP packages in the Packagist repository. The malicious payload injected links to fraudulent casinos into sites that used these packages and, on iOS devices only, a hidden iframe that loaded the DarkSword exploit kit. The attack delivered a spyware module that stole keychain contents, Wi-Fi passwords, SMS messages, photos, and other personal data. Other modules found in this campaign were used to steal crypto wallet data and the seed phrases used to recover them.

SlowMist researchers found the same DarkSword exploit chain used in a fake app, FomoPeek. FomoPeek was published in the App Store, presenting itself as a crypto wallet tracker. The malware was designed to steal data from notes and crypto wallet apps.

Also in August, we discovered infected versions of popular iOS apps distributed through Telegram (link in Russian). To install such an app, the attackers asked users to buy a developer certificate. The modified versions contained a malicious module that collected device information, took screenshots, and sent this data to a server.

Mobile threat statistics

The downward trend in attacks on mobile devices involving malware, adware, or unwanted software continued: the number fell to 1,668,368 in Q3 from 1,996,823 in Q2.
