Full Text:
Introduction

A couple of months ago, our research revealed a highly sophisticated infection chain and a complex .NET assembly-loading framework built on XAML markup, which strongly indicates a supply-chain attack targeting a custom Windows build used exclusively by government entities in Asia. The malicious framework has been labeled NetamLoader; at present, no attribution to any known APT group has been established.

The sample came to light in the first half of 2026, when Kaspersky Security Network (KSN) issued a malware detection alert for a .config file using AppDomainManager injection to load arbitrary .NET assemblies. The file was packaged inside a CAB archive placed in the directory that stores Windows operating system update packages. Initial analysis of the CAB contents found no malicious code: most executables were legitimate components of the third-party patch management tool Patch My PC, and even the .NET assemblies used for the injection were Microsoft-signed. A later re-examination of the original .config file and the full loading process revealed the infection chain and framework described in this report.

Kaspersky’s products detect this threat as HEUR:Trojan.MSIL.NetamLoader.gen, Trojan.MSIL.Zapchast.*, and Trojan.Script.Agent.*.

Background

During routine threat hunting, KSN sent us a malware detection alert. The notification flagged a .config file that employed AppDomainManager injection to load arbitrary .NET assemblies. The file was compressed into a CAB archive named e4537a1762fcafd2fd96bfc825bad34f9db9a24d and saved in the folder that stores Windows operating system update packages. Below is the full path to this archive:

C:\Windows\SoftwareDistribution\Download\e4537a1762fcafd2fd96bfc825bad34f9db9a24d

Starting with this CAB archive, we uncovered a highly complex infection chain that uses a previously unknown advanced loading framework.

Initial infection

The CAB file contains the following seven files, which are extracted and placed in the path C:\Windows\SoftwareDistribution\Download\Install\:

Files compressed in the CAB file

Except for Resources.resx, none of the files contain malicious code. We did not observe how the CAB file was delivered to the victim; we only saw the process PatchMyPC-ScriptRunner.exe running with the following arguments:

C:\Windows\SoftwareDistribution\Download\Install\PatchMyPC-ScriptRunner.exe -updatepackage -applicationid=xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx

After the file is launched in this manner, the infection chain progresses to stage 1.

Stage 1

Starting with the execution of PatchMyPC-ScriptRunner.exe, which then served as a host process for loading several payloads, we identified a complex two‑stage loading mechanism with multiple steps. The overall flow of stage 1 is summarized in the diagram below.

Infection chain: Stage 1

Step 1

The AppDomainManager injection technique is used to load an arbitrary .NET assembly. With this mechanism, when PatchMyPC-ScriptRunner.exe runs, the accompanying configuration file PatchMyPC-ScriptRunner.exe.config in the same directory is loaded before the executable’s main function runs. Below is the content of PatchMyPC‑ScriptRunner.exe.config.

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8" ?> <configuration> <runtime> <appDomainManagerType value="Microsoft.ApplicationServer.Caching.DataCacheFactoryConfiguration"> </appDomainManagerType> <appDomainManagerAssembly value="Microsoft.HostIntegration.Connectors, Version=1.0.0.0, Culture=neutral, PublicKeyToken=31bf3856ad364e35"> </appDomainManagerAssembly> <NGenAssemblyUsageLog enabled="0" /> </runtime> <startup> <supportedRuntime version="v4.0" sku=".NETFramework,Version=v4.6" /> </startup> </configuration>

According to the configuration file, the class Microsoft.ApplicationServer.Caching.DataCacheFactoryConfiguration from the Microsoft.HostIntegration.Connectors.dll module (a Microsoft‑signed assembly) is loaded. DataCacheFactoryConfiguration is the configuration class for the Windows Server AppFabric Cache Client, specifying the settings for a new cache client. When the configuration class is loaded, its instance first attempts to find and read the default configuration file, fabric.config, located in the same directory. The contents of fabric.config are shown below:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?> <section name="foo"> <customType className="System.Resources.ResXResourceSet, System.Windows.Forms, Version=4.0.0.0, Culture=neutral, PublicKeyToken=b77a5c561934e089(Resources.resx)" /> </section>

Step 2

The DataCacheFactoryConfiguration class has a design flaw that can be abused to load arbitrary assemblies. The fabric.config file is meticulously crafted. When the file is loaded, the DataCacheFactoryConfiguration instance examines its className attribute, loads the specified type (System.Resources.ResXResourceSet from the System.Windows.Forms assembly), and creates a ResXResourceSet instance, passing “Resources.resx” to its constructor for parsing.

In the .resx file, multiple layers of payloads – including several XAML files, .NET assemblies, and JSON data – are encoded, compressed, or encrypted (see the diagram below). Each layer is unpacked and loaded by the layer above it. Once a layer finishes its operation, the next layer is extracted and loaded. Below, we analyze each layer in the order in which it is loaded:

Multiple layers of payloads are compressed and encrypted in the .resx file

The Microsoft RESX schema defines the XML layout used by .resx files, which has a human-readable structure and can hold application resources: strings, images, icons, and serialized objects. The Resources.resx file contains a Base64‑encoded binary object that was serialized using the well‑known, highly vulnerable .NET BinaryFormatter class.

Base64-encoded serialized binary object in Resources.resx

Parsing this .resx file with ResXResourceSet causes the embedded Base64‑encoded binary payload to invoke BinaryFormatter.Deserialize(), triggering a deserialization vulnerability that enables a TypeConfuseDelegate attack. The TypeConfuseDelegate then invokes XamlReader.Parse(), which loads a XAML payload (named XAML-1) embedded within the binary object.

XAML is a markup language for building user interfaces in .NET applications, but its capabilities extend far beyond that. Using two built‑in objects, ObjectDataProvider and ResourceDictionary, logic equivalent to C# code can be expressed in an XML‑like syntax.

A code snippet of XAML-1

Step 3

The XAML-1 code acts as a loader for an embedded payload. The process is as follows:

Retrieve the full command line of the current host process PatchMyPC‑ScriptRunner.exe, converting all arguments to lowercase.

Generate the AES key by hashing the command‑line string with SHA‑256.

Decode the Base64 string embedded in XAML-1 into a binary array. Use the first 16 bytes of that array as the IV, then decrypt the remaining encrypted data with AES. The decrypted output is another piece of XAML code, which we refer to as XAML-2.

Load XAML-2 into memory using the .NET API System.Windows.Markup.XamlReader.Load().

If any exception occurs during decryption, trigger Environment.Exit(0), silently terminating the host process to prevent error messages that might reveal the attack.

Stage 2

XAML‑2 initiates stage 2 of the infection. The diagram below shows the overall flow of this stage.

Infection chain: Stage 2

XAML‑2 contains two embedded Base64‑encoded sections. These sections are actually two additional XAML files (referred to as XAML-2-1 and XAML-2-2) that were first compressed with ZIP and then encoded in Base64. After decoding and decompressing, XAML-2 loads each file into memory separately with XamlReader.Load().

A code snippet of XAML-2

XAML-2-1

The first file consists of 796 lines. Its sole purpose is to hijack a key AMSI API to bypass anti‑malware scanning.

Sensitive strings in XAML-2-1 are cut into tiny pieces

To avoid detection by anti‑malware signature scans, sensitive strings are split into very short fragments. When XAML-2-1 is loaded and parsed, the fragments are reassembled into the original string.

The key steps it takes to achieve its goal are as follows:

Check the OS architecture by verifying whether IntPtr.Size equals 8. If it does not, the host process isn’t 64‑bit, so abort the hijack operation.

Combine the split strings into a single CLSID GUID (fdb00e52-a214-4aa1-8fba-4357bb0072ec), then try to create an instance of the AMSI COM object using this GUID.

Patch the AMSI module.

Create a delegate for the runtime method Console.Clear() and then obtain its native function pointer. Next, patch the method by overwriting its first bytes in memory with the binary payload (41 C7 00 01 00 00 00 33 C0 C3).

Obtain the native pointer of the AMSI COM object with Marshal.GetIUnknownForObject(). From this pointer, read the address of its virtual method table and add 0x18 to reach another pointer that holds the address of the CAmsiAntimalware::Scan method.

Use VirtualProtect() to make the Scan() pointer writable, change its value from the address of the CAmsiAntimalware::Scan() method to the address of the patched Console.Clear(), and then restore the pointer’s original protection attributes. Once this step is complete, every scan returns AMSI_RESULT_CLEAN (value = 0).

One patch targets the Console.Clear() API, which resides in the memory space of an existing legitimate module, while the other modifies only the virtual tables of the AMSI module, allowing the malware to pass code integrity checks.

XAML-2-2

XAML-2-2 consists of two parts: a .NET module (the first loader, .NET 1 Loader) and a JSON data payload (the C2 configuration, JSON-1). Both components are compressed with ZIP and then encoded in Base64. XAML-2-2 first decodes and decompresses the .NET assembly .NET 1 Loader, then uses the Assembly.CreateInstance() API to create an instance of the .NET 1 Loader and passes the Base64‑encoded JSON-1 to the m.C() method of .NET 1 Loader as a parameter.

.NET 1 Loader

.NET 1 Loader decodes, decompresses, and parses JSON‑1. The decoded and decompressed JSON‑1 is shown below:

{ "p": "[Base64‑encoded JSON, which we call JSON‑1-p]" "c": "[Base64‑encoded JSON, which we call JSON‑1-c]" }

oub: Base64‑encoded XAML that invokes Exit(0)

After obtaining the configuration, .NET 1 Loader proceeds with the following key steps:

Delete the update records from the system log related to the malicious update packages, along with the malicious files and cache files used in stage 1.

Delete malicious files extracted from the CAB

PatchMyPC-ScriptRunner.exe.config fabric.config Resources.resx

Delete CLR usage logs and Windows system Prefetch cache files to eliminate evidence that could be used in forensic analysis.

%LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\CLR_v4.0\UsageLogs\PatchMyPC-ScriptRunner.exe.log %WINDIR%\Prefetch\PATCHMYPC-SCRIPTRUNNER.EXE-*.pf

Read the files’ contents, filter out any lines containing the exact substring GetExtendedUpdateInfoHandler, and write the filtered content back to the log files. The path contains the keyword CmitUpdateAgent, which may be linked to a custom Windows 10 build used by a government in Asia.

"%WINDIR%\Logs\CmitUpdateAgent\20????\20??????"

The algorithm that generates the GUID path is unique– it derives the GUID from the C2 URL– so each C2 server has its own distinct set of bound GUIDs. Of the nine GUIDs derived using this method, one indicates that an exception occurred, and the others are numbered 0 through 7. For example, when the malware catches exception code 129, it creates the registry subkey {bde7ddc2-1f6f-4397-a0df-ae7c7d67d65a} to indicate that an exception occurred. It then checks the bit mask, where 129 equals binary 10000001. Consequently, it creates the eighth subkey {74084115-433e-4fe8-8d01-41c48fbfeef6} and the first subkey {bf6f4bde-97db-4dcd-9546-7ebf10061519}.

Verify that each necessary configuration item exists in JSON-1-p, then validate some of its items against hardcoded values. If any item fails the check, halt the infection chain and submit the execution result to the reporting C2 server.

Verify that the current user is an administrator; if not, throw an exception with code 128.

Check whether the configuration item aop exists. If it does, Base64-decode its value, use the result as XAML-3, and skip to step 9.

Generate a unique malware instance ID for the configuration item ii by calling Guid.NewGuid().

Query the SusClientId value from the registry key SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\WindowsUpdate. Then generate the value for the newly defined configuration item si by computing a GUID using the same algorithm as above. Use the concatenation of the retrieved SusClientId value and the byte sequence \x14\x43\x9B\x64 as the input data for the algorithm.

Parse JSON-1-p, extract the relevant items and their values, and convert them to XAML format. Next, follow the steps outlined in the XAML-3 section to generate the complex XAML script XAML-3.

Create a COM instance of WScript.Shell (CLSID: 41904400-BE18-11D3-A28B-00104BD35090) and retrieve the environment of the current process. Then set the COMPlus_ETWEnabled environment variable to 0 to prevent the CLR from registering the .NET ETW provider, which hides the associated events.

Use RPC to create a remote COM object (CLSID: ab8902b4-09ca-4bb6-b78d-a8f59079a8d5). Exploit it via an unknown binary object deserialization vulnerability and the TypeConfuseDelegate technique. Once the exploit succeeds, XAML-3 is loaded into the remote host process dllhost.exe. This is a covert method for initiating a new process that loads the malicious payload XAML‑3. This technique effectively separates the infection chain from its initial process, allowing it to bypass behavioral monitoring by security solutions such as EDR.

The execution result (in JSON format, shown below) is first AES‑encrypted using the key from the item e. A randomly generated IV is prepended to the encrypted data, and the result is then Base64‑encoded.

[ { // Fixed value "_": "0202097a-5c1e-460d-b5e0-030b9756b242", // Error number: 0 indicates successful execution "e": "0 ", // Value of config "ii" "i": "94aafd58-c00c-402a-aae6-858b4486a1a4" } ]

XAML-3

XAML-3 is a critical payload that, after leaving the original process tree, is loaded and executed in a different process: dllhost.exe. XAML-3 is generated from template XAML-3. As shown in the diagram below, the template is decoded and decrypted using the value of the ibi item in JSON-1-p. In addition to template XAML‑3, the final decryption includes two other XAML templates (template __P1__ and template __P2__).

The multi-layer encryption structure of “ibi”

The AES key is taken from the config item ibk. The first 16 bytes of the encrypted binary data serve as AES IV 1. After decryption, the data consists of a simple header followed by AES IV 2.

Template XAML‑3 includes two string placeholders, __P1__ and __P2__. Each placeholder is replaced with compressed, Base64‑encoded XAML (template __P1__ and XAML‑P2).

The content of template __P1__ is identical to XAML-2-1 and bypasses AMSI in the new process. XAML-P2 is generated from the template __P2__.

Some of the item values in template __P2__ come from the C2 configuration data in JSON-1-p. Within template __P2__, the placeholder __P__ is replaced with a compressed, encoded payload – the .NET 2 Plugin – which is decoded from the oib value in JSON-1-p. After completing all the operations, the template __P2__ becomes XAML-P2.

The C2 configuration in XAML‑P2 is shown below:

When dllhost.exe loads XAML-3, it loads template __P1__ and XAML-P2 one by one. Finally, XAML-P2 decodes and decompresses the embedded payload (.NET 2 Plugin), loads the .NET 2 Plugin into the current domain, and then calls the plugin’s entry method, m.C().

.NET 2 Plugin

This payload is a .NET assembly (PE file). As discussed above, it is loaded by XAML-P2 into the host process dllhost.exe. In the plugin’s entry method m.C(), a thread is spawned to execute the malicious operations.

The following key steps are executed in this thread:

Configuration initialization: Load the C2 configuration from the current AppDomain’s data storage and assign it to the corresponding member variables.

Gather system information from the registry:

"HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\NET Framework Setup\NDP\v4\full", Key="Version" "HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion", Key="BuildLab"

AES encryption scheme for network traffic

All traffic between the malware and the C2 server is encrypted and authenticated using AES‑128‑CBC with HMAC. The encryption and authentication keys are derived from a master key – specified in the configuration as "ec"="9fT04e03tAiZAPogcDWt0w==" – by applying HMAC with distinct seed values.

For a given master key and a single-byte seed, the derivation works as follows:

Generate a 16‑byte sequence from the seed; this serves as the HMAC key.

Compute HMAC‑SHA256 over the master key to obtain an intermediate key.

Use this intermediate key as the HMAC key to compute HMAC‑SHA256 on the constant byte 0x01.

Take the first 16 bytes of the resulting hash; this becomes the final derived key.

Accordingly, the server-side encryption and decryption keys mirror those on the client (malware) side.

The code implements an encapsulation of AES-CBC encryption combined with HMAC-SHA256 integrity verification. It uses a randomly generated IV to symmetrically encrypt the plaintext in CBC mode and produces ciphertext. Next, it calculates an SHA256 message authentication code for the concatenated “IV+ciphertext” using a separate HMAC key. Finally, it concatenates the three segments – IV (16 bytes) | ciphertext | HMAC (32 bytes) – into a single byte array that constitutes the final encrypted message. This follows the standard cryptographic Encrypt-then-MAC construction. The receiver must validate the HMAC before decrypting with the corresponding key and IV, which ensures confidentiality, integrity, and tamper resistance.

Discovering proxies

.NET 2 Plugin detects the system proxy using three methods:

Retrieve the system‑wide proxy configuration using the Win32 WinHTTP API function WinHttpGetDefaultProxyConfiguration(), then extract the proxy server with the regular expression (?:([a-zA-Z]+)=)?(.*).

If that fails, locate the running explorer.exe process, impersonate its access token using Impersonate(), and retrieve its proxy configuration with the .NET API WebProxy.GetDefaultProxy().

If both methods fail, fall back to obtaining the proxy from the .NET property DefaultWebProxy.

These methods ensure that the malware can reach external networks even in complex network environments with proxies.

Execute downloaded XAML payload in an isolated AppDomain

This technique abuses MulticastDelegate again by using reflection to modify its private _invocationList array. .NET 2 Plugin creates a multicast delegate (CrossAppDomainDelegate) and replaces one entry in its invocation list with a malicious delegate pointing to XamlReader.Parse(). When AppDomain.DoCallBack() executes this multicast delegate, it iterates through the invocation list and invokes the injected XamlReader.Parse() to parse and execute the downloaded XAML.

In more detail, the process is as follows:

Create a new isolated AppDomain with a randomly generated GUID as its name.

Copy all configuration data from the current AppDomain into the new one.

Set the proxy information in the new AppDomain and assign it to the variable px.

Use TypeConfuseDelegate to replace TimeZoneInfo.ClearCachedData() with XamlReader.Parse(), thereby modifying the MulticastDelegate(CrossAppDomainDelegate).

Use appDomain.DoCallBack() to invoke XamlReader.Parse() within the isolated AppDomain, executing the downloaded XAML payload.

Transfer any updated configuration data from the new AppDomain back to the original AppDomain.

Unload the isolated AppDomain to complete the cleanup.

This technique keeps the downloaded malicious payload out of the main AppDomain, which increases stability and allows the payload to be fully cleaned up after execution.

Infrastructure

The attack relies on commercial hosting infrastructure. The C2 IP is part of Cloudflare’s CDN, and the domain name is registered with Cloudflare.

Victims

Based on KSN telemetry data, we identified a single victim in Asia. Additionally, we learned that the malware was designed to target a specially customized government‑only version of the Windows operating system. Consequently, we infer that the victims are Asian government entities.

Attribution

After analyzing the TTPs, code similarities, and infrastructure, we were unable to link the attack to any known APT group.

Conclusions

Technological sovereignty has become a global trend. In today’s geopolitical climate, a growing number of countries are building their own core software platforms, including operating systems, databases, middleware, and cloud services, with operating systems often the top priority. The advantage is that each country controls the development, operation, and upgrading of its own operating systems, granting it full autonomy over the entire process. On the other hand, it also means that each country must protect this entire vast ecosystem on its own. Bringing the operation and maintenance of such a system to maturity is a lengthy process. Until then, both the system and its emerging supply chain could be exposed to attacks through multiple vectors, increasing potential vulnerabilities.

Title: Weak keys in eMudhra CA certificates: the risks and how to respond | Kaspersky official blog
Context: We’ve seen forged or stolen certificates abused by the DarkHotel APT and the Flame malware, and in 2011 we saw attack attempts after the certificate authority Comodo was...
Full Text:
Certificates both protect TLS connections and digitally sign applications, and forged ones turn up in real-world attacks from time to time. We’ve seen forged or stolen certificates abused by the DarkHotel APT and the Flame malware, and in 2011 we saw attack attempts after the certificate authority Comodo was compromised. Pulling off this trick usually takes serious expertise. But attacking eMudhra certificates in 2026 doesn’t take much effort at all. An attacker just has to guess a number from 1 to 255. Private keys for intermediate certificate authorities are normally gigantic numbers. But in this case, eight of them were the following: 4, 56, 66, 115, 155, 156, 230, and 237. They could be guessed using the public keys (available in public certificates) in under a second. As a result, a hypothetical attacker could issue certificates for anything by signing them with one of the compromised private keys.

Six of these keys were meant for issuing TLS certificates, and the other two were for code signing. All eight intermediate certificate authorities (CAs) were also cross-signed by the Sectigo CA. This means clients with different trust chains could trust a forged certificate.

The major browsers have already blocked the dangerous certificate chains. But IT and security teams still need to assess and remediate the risk in many other systems across their organizations. Scripts for scheduled data-processing, corporate NGFWs, monitoring servers, applications with built-in certificate stores, and devices that don’t get regular updates may accept forged certificates and be vulnerable to man-in-the-middle (MitM) attacks. The keys needed for this are already built into publicly available interception tools.

Timeline of the eMudhra certificate authority incident

The problematic keys came from a batch of 24 intermediate CAs that eMudhra created on April 30, 2025. Instead of cryptographically random values for a 384-bit elliptic curve, eight of the keys turned out to be small numbers. According to eMudhra’s own description, a “key wrap/unwrap step” during key generation created a second, weak set of keys. Because keys are created and stored in a dedicated device called a hardware security module (HSM), a weak key is hard to notice on its own. It’s still unclear what error caused the keys to be generated twice and the weak set to be used; the investigation is ongoing.

In May 2025, the Sectigo CA signed all eight intermediate certificates. Then, on October 17, 2026, an independent researcher notified the security teams at Mozilla, Google, and Apple, as well as the CA itself, that the keys were recoverable. On October 20, Mozilla publicly disclosed the incident. This means that for almost a year and a half the keys could have been recovered and certificates forged.

On October 22, eMudhra announced that it was exiting the global SSL/TLS certificate business.

What an attacker can do

Using the vulnerable intermediate CAs, an attacker can sign a forged certificate for someone else’s domain. Clients that still trust that chain and have no other safeguards will take the forgery for the real server.

A certificate alone isn’t enough to intercept HTTPS traffic. The attacker also needs a way to tamper with the victim’s traffic or redirect the connection. That’s possible, for example, in a compromised office network, on a Wi-Fi access point the attacker controls, or by interfering with routing and DNS. And all of this does happen in the wild, as the DarkHotel attacks, among others, have shown.

There’s one more danger: two of the keys can be used for code signing. In theory, that would let an attacker deliver malware that appears to come from a trusted vendor and doesn’t trigger scary OS warnings during installation.

Was it exploited?

Experts from various companies who analyzed the after-effects of the incident haven’t found any malicious attacks that used these certificates. eMudhra and CERT-In have also reported finding no abuse. The Chrome team found no certificates from the six CAs in public Certificate Transparency logs.

This means that systems where browsers check certificates through Certificate Transparency (CT) were most likely not attacked. But many devices and applications — especially servers and IoT devices, don’t check CT at all, so we can’t say anything about them. Today, malicious actors no longer need to write their own hacking tools to pull off an attack like this. Version 12.3 of mitmproxy — a popular tool among security researchers — already has built-in support for compromised keys.

Where the risk has been eliminated, and where that isn’t guaranteed

Major platforms quickly revoked the compromised certificates. As early as October 17, Chrome did so through CRLSets, and Firefox — through OneCRL. On October 18, eMudhra itself revoked the certificates, citing “CA Compromise”. Apple took action on October 19, and the Sectigo CA also revoked the cross-signed copies. Microsoft revoked the certificates on October 20. Depending on the settings of a specific application and OS, revocation may have taken effect even without an application update, since blocklists are often updated separately.

At the same time, a more radical measure is under way: withdrawing trust from the root CA. Chrome has announced the planned removal of “emSign ECC Root CA – G3” from the browser. Certificates issued under the “emSign Root CA – G1” root, and the root itself, aren’t affected. According to eMudhra’s estimate, about 30 000 certificates will need to be migrated.

But certificate revocation only works where the client can find out about the revocation to then be able to actually act upon it. Many applications check the signature, server name, and certificate validity period, but don’t retrieve or update blocklists. Here are the typical cases:

Outdated and LTS systems. LTS (long-term support) status alone doesn’t mean a system is vulnerable. By definition, a system with this status receives support. But old containers, frozen OS images, and systems that are no longer updated can keep trusting revoked CAs for a long time. It all depends on updates to ca-certificates and TLS libraries, and the settings of the specific application.

Automated systems and servers. On emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com — a site created by enthusiasts where you can check any client software for misplaced trust — curl and Zabbix dominate the list of the most vulnerable systems. For HTTP checks, Zabbix usually uses libcurl and the certificate store configured for it. Similar behavior is also documented in the built-in curl in macOS. At the OS level and in Safari, the certificate is revoked, but curl reads a plain /etc/ssl/cert.pem file, and that’s precisely where the fix has to be made. This is a good example: even when system-level trust and revocation mechanisms work, individual applications — including ones that ship with the OS by default — can remain vulnerable.

Python, Ruby, Go, Java, and containers. An application may use its own set of root CAs, which isn’t updated along with the OS. Endor Labs found more than 25 popular packages that contain the affected root.

Slack, GitHub Desktop, and other apps built on the Electron framework. These apps ship with their own Electron/Chromium, so updating a separately installed Chrome doesn’t update Slack. The certificate revocations are already in the new Electron version, but now every developer has to rebuild and distribute their app, and every user has to install the update. That said, not every Electron app is necessarily vulnerable. The outcome depends on the version, how the app updates its blocklists, and which network stack it uses.

Mobile browsers and IoT devices. Mobile Chrome, Firefox, and Safari get certificate revocation data as quickly as their desktop counterparts do. With the stock browsers from smartphone makers, this isn’t the case. In a published test, Samsung Browser 31.0.0.64 accepted all six test chains from emSign while rejecting the ones from Sectigo. For HarmonyOS 6 and 7, researchers found the affected CAs in Huawei’s published list of root CAs, and those CAs can’t be revoked manually.

For unsupported devices, home appliances, and old firmware, a certificate store update may never be released. In those cases, the problem could linger for years.

Impact on TLS inspection in a corporate network

When an NGFW or web gateway inspects encrypted traffic, it maintains two connections: one with the client and the other with the external server. The client receives a certificate signed by the corporate CA, while the gateway itself verifies the authenticity of the external server.

If the gateway accepts a forged eMudhra certificate, even an updated browser on an employee’s computer won’t see the dangerous chain. Instead, it will receive the familiar corporate certificate. In this scenario, the security tool itself hides the problem from the client. That said, carrying out such an attack would also require intercepting traffic.

To fix the validation policy and certificate lists on the inspection device itself, follow the vendor’s instructions — if the vendor has published any, that is.

At Cisco, the status of the issue is documented in detail for all products. Most of them are still listed as “under investigation”, but mitigation measures are recommended for vulnerable devices.

Sophos and Check Point promise device software updates and, in the meantime, advise removing the certificates manually. Neither company has published a security advisory, but employees of each posted recommendations on its support forum.

For Fortinet devices, instructions for checking and removing emSign certificates can be found here. Palo Alto offered only general advice instead of specifics for its own products.

Of course, a properly configured gateway can indeed temporarily protect outdated client devices that trust the dangerous certificates.

To check specific devices, services, containers, and virtual machines, you can use a dedicated website. One possible scenario for proactively hunting for threats that exploit or have previously exploited weak keys is described here.

Title: Cybersecurity in Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey | Kaspersky official blog
Context: First comes the bay of Lamos, where the giant Laestrygonians launch a DDoS attack, hurling requests rocks at the Greeks and wiping out nearly all of Odysseus’ infrastructure crew
Full Text:
We’ve looked at information-security cases and technologies through the lens of famous movies, popular book series, and even fairy tales more than once before. Next up it’s the turn of Christopher Nolan’s adaptation of The Odyssey (based on the ancient Greek epic poem), which, incidentally, inspired the works of Tolkien, various movies and series in the Star Wars franchise, and much more.

Homer’s Odyssey doesn’t just describe classic plots and archetypes. It also covers key technologies and principles of digital hygiene — albeit in veiled form. The hero’s journey was a risky business — and so, for that matter, is watching The Odyssey itself, but we’ll get to that at the end of this post. For now, let’s see how to safely sail the vast internet Hellenic seas in search of Ithaca.

Administrator Penelope and 108 attackers

Nolan has reshaped the poem’s structure quite a bit, but the film still opens on the island of Ithaca. There, Penelope and Telemachus, the wife and son of Odysseus, king of Ithaca, wait for him to return from the Trojan War. Meanwhile, a mob of 108 suitors is running riot in Odysseus’ house. They’re all courting Penelope and dreaming of the throne, and the whole kingdom is on the brink of collapse.

In essence, this is an attack on digital infrastructure by a group of malicious actors. Penelope, an advanced user with admin rights, does everything she can to block attempts to hack the root account take Odysseus’ place. Her trick: she’s promised to choose a husband only after she finishes weaving a burial shroud for Odysseus’ father, Laertes. By day, she weaves in front of everyone. By night, she unravels everything she’s done: clearly a daily factory reset.

Nolan gives Penelope even more authority than Homer did. This helps highlight the coming-of-age story of Telemachus, who starts out as a beginner user. His storyline is about searching for his father and recognizing him: the ancient Greek version of multi-factor authentication. Following the tradition set by James Joyce, Nolan focuses on the tragedy of Telemachus, who can’t remember Odysseus, since his father last connected to the server left Ithaca so long ago.

Root account Odysseus, Trojan Horse, and Ram VPN

Meanwhile, Odysseus is on the island of the nymph Calypso. She feeds him lotus flowers that make him gradually lose his memory — clearly the classic playbook of ransomware. But in seven years, Calypso never manages to fully encrypt wipe his memory. Odysseus longs for home, and the hapless ransomware operator ends up helping him partly recover the encrypted data remember his story. Odysseus remembers how, after ten years of war outside the walls of Troy, he came up with a cunning scheme that became the basis for all Trojan horses ever since…

The Greeks left a malicious file huge wooden horse on the shore and sailed away. A spy who stayed behind convinced the Trojans that it was a very useful thing an offering to Athena, and they dragged the horse into the city. At night, once the people of Troy had gone into sleep mode, the malicious modules soldiers led by Odysseus hidden inside the horse added themselves to Defender’s exclusions opened the gates. The Greeks returned and captured Troy, then stole data and cryptocurrency burned and looted the city. Only after that did they finally head home.

But the road to Ithaca was long and dangerous. After landing on an unfamiliar island, Odysseus got overconfident. Instead of leaving the suspicious site stocking up and sailing away, he went off to explore the infrastructure, and ended up trapped with his men in the cave of a giant Cyclops, known online as Polyphemus. The Greeks managed to blind the Cyclops, though not without losses, and Odysseus figured out how to get out of the cave: by hiding under the bellies of the rams. The blinded Cyclops felt the rams’ wool but never noticed the Greeks — a textbook example of how a VPN works.

But once he’s out of the cave, Odysseus gets cocky and fires an arrow at Polyphemus. That gives away his real IP address location, and his crew has to flee in a hurry from the furious Cyclops. In the end, the ships are knocked off course and get lost at sea.

Interestingly, unlike in the film, Homer’s poem has a group of OLYMP experts constantly steering the course of events. For example, Odysseus’ ships lost their way because of the interference of Poseidon, OLYMP’s chief expert in maritime technology. As we know from the poem, Odysseus first logged in to Polyphemus’ place as “Nub_Oddy”, but later, in a fit of arrogance, changed his username to “Odysseus_Son_of_Laertes_King_of_Ithaca”. With Odysseus deanonymized, the Cyclops used the Pray messaging app to send Poseidon a voice request to launch targeted attacks on Odysseus’ crew. In Nolan’s version, though, Poseidon doesn’t appear as a character. Instead, he becomes a metaphor for an APT a destructive force of nature.

Expert Circe, APT group Sirena, Scylla, and Charybdis malware

Odysseus’ ships drift across the vast Web seas, and every so often they land on unsafe sites shores. First comes the bay of Lamos, where the giant Laestrygonians launch a DDoS attack, hurling requests rocks at the Greeks and wiping out nearly all of Odysseus’ infrastructure crew. Only he and a small group survive.

Next, the heroes land on the island of a lone cybersecurity professional known as Circe, who puts them through harsh cybersecurity training. She lures Odysseus’ warriors to dinner with a social engineering scheme known as pig butchering and turns them into… yes, you guessed it, pigs. But the protagonist doesn’t fall for her tricks, so Circe agrees to help him and gives his crew their human form back. She also advises Odysseus to run an analysis in an isolated environment descend into Hades’ underworld and find the blind Tiresias, whom the OLYMP experts promoted to threat intelligence analyst gifted with foresight.

Tiresias tells Odysseus that he is the only one with enough cybersecurity knowledge strength to reach Ithaca. But Odysseus is determined to save his crew. He learns that they’ll have to face a very dangerous APT group, the Sirens. They use advanced social engineering (singing) to lure sailors to their doom. So Odysseus orders his men to put in solid protection against voice spam: wax earplugs. The film never lets us hear what the Sirens actually sing. They may well be posing as bank employees, law enforcement, or government officials, but the anti-spam trick keeps the crew safe.

Then far more destructive malware hits the ship: Scylla and Charybdis. From Tiresias’ beginner course in infosec, Odysseus knows that Scylla has six heads, and can hit no more than six users at a time. But dodging her attack means running straight into Charybdis, who will deal critical damage drag the whole ship into a whirlpool. This is the first historical mention of an ethical thought experiment that would later become known as the “trolley problem” — and Odysseus picks Scylla.

Having passed these threats, the remaining crew members land on the island of Thrinacia. That cluster allows initial login with a standard access level for regular users, on one condition: don’t touch the island’s critical resource, the sacred bulls of Helios — chief expert in solar technology. But the warriors ignore Odysseus’ instructions, break the rule, and use that resource to mine food. This triggers a defense system built by OLYMP’s leader, nicknamed Zeus, which permanently blocks strikes down the ship and Odysseus’ crew. Odysseus himself barely survives and reaches Calypso’s island.

Return of root

Once his memory is back, Odysseus builds a raft and charts a course, thanks to Calypso. Athena, the wisest of the OLYMP experts, helps him reach the shores of Ithaca against all odds. He then slips into the city disguised as a beggar.

There, Odysseus passes several steps of multi-factor authentication:

His old dog Argus sees his master, wags his tail, and dies.

Telemachus sees this and realizes the poor wanderer is his father.

His elderly nurse Eurycleia recognizes the man she raised by a unique code the scar on his leg.

But that isn’t enough to restore his root access. So with Telemachus’ help, Odysseus has to enter the palace using the account of one of his former companions, where he meets the administrator, Penelope. Nolan added an important twist here. At this moment, Odysseus regrets creating the first Trojan, which destroyed the infrastructure of an entire city. He also realizes that the malicious suitors’ constant attempts to guess the root password put Ithaca’s infrastructure at risk of the same decline.

Penelope begins to guess who is standing in front of her from his digital footprint indirect signs. She then sets a condition for the would-be root account owners her suitors: she’ll marry the one who can shoot an arrow through the rings of 12 axes with Odysseus’ bow. The bow is essentially a passkey with biometrics, which nobody knew how to fake back in those ancient times. So the bad actors fail one after another. Only Odysseus draws the bowstring and sends an arrow through every axe’s ring. Thanks to the successful biometric authentication, everyone accepts him as the true root king of Ithaca.

The rest is simple: the malware villains are neutralized, the kingdom is saved, and peace and information security return to Ithaca.

Why watching The Odyssey can be dangerous

In the window between the movie stopping being shown in cinemas and its release on digital media, our experts discovered a new multi-stage malicious campaign that had been running since mid-August. Malicious actors are spreading a previously unknown piece of malware called MovieReaper through compromised torrent trackers. They disguise it as downloads of popular movies — first and foremost The Odyssey, one of the biggest premieres of the summer. Scammers use this irresistible bait to make people more likely to download their file. The malware itself is as treacherous as the Sirens. It can hide from detection, give attackers remote access to the victim’s device, and deploy extra modules to stay in the system even after it’s removed. Read the full technical breakdown of MovieReaper on our expert blog, Securelist. Victims of this attack have been found all over the world. This is one more reminder of how important it is to be careful online — especially when downloading files.

Practical lessons from The Odyssey

So what can we learn from the story of the cunning king of Ithaca?

A good offense isn’t the best defense. Instead of developing software to attack other users, focus on your own information security.

Keep an eye on your personal data. It can fall into the hands of bad actors, which can lead to targeted attacks.

Set up multi-factor authentication. It lowers the risk of being hacked, and helps you regain access to your accounts safely.

Set up reliable protection (and don’t ignore it), because you should beware Greeks bearing gifts!

Title: Technology that blocks DGA domains | Kaspersky official blog
Context: But the first thing our email products focus on is the “From” field
Full Text:
We use many technologies to detect email spam. They analyze every part of a message: headers, text, images, and links. But the first thing our email products focus on is the “From” field. If the address contains a domain that’s already on our denylist, it’s an easy call. But spammers know the drill, so they register domains in industrial quantities to make emails, even from a single campaign, arrive from completely different addresses. Clearly, they don’t do that by hand. The process has long been automated, and attackers’ algorithms can register huge numbers of domains in a matter of minutes. But every domain needs a name. Coming up with a unique one for each isn’t feasible. So spammers use domain generation algorithms (DGAs), which create similar names with minor variations, based on date and time, pseudo-random numbers, and so on.

In fact, to block mailings such as these, you don’t need every address on your denylist. We’re good at automating processes, too. For some time now, our email solutions have included a technology that detects domains generated by DGAs, and shuts down entire batch with a single rule. Let me explain how this technology works.

How we detect and block generated domain names in bulk

As soon as any of our technologies flags an email as spam, its address becomes subject to further examination. If it meets a number of criteria, its domain is added to our database of domains we consider “bad”. We built a cascade of classifiers that compares these domains by similarity, groups them into clusters, and creates a short but comprehensive rule that blocks the entire cluster. Our email protection solutions receive this rule with an update. From then on, they block all emails sent from addresses on any domain that matches it — even if those domains have never been used in spam campaigns yet.

Here’s a real-world example. Let’s say the classifier flags several lookalike domains in a collection of “bad” ones it has gathered:

sxkjcc.asia

sxkjcd.asia

sxkjcy.asia

Then, one rule is enough to catch them all: @sxkjc[a-z0-9]\.asia\b

How to protect your company from spam

According to our analysis, 44.9% of emails sent last year were spam. Unwanted, unsolicited emails distract employees, waste working time, and clog inboxes. In some cases, they also contain scam, phishing, or malware content. To protect business customers from this deluge of threats, our solutions for corporate email security have anti-spam technologies that we constantly improve. This includes the technology described above for blocking domains generated by DGAs.
